title: Why Hood Canal runs out of breath
teaches: A fjord's slow flushing, and how new ocean water lifts the old water to the surface
summary: **Hood Canal is a fjord.** A trough about 110 km long cut by ice, up to about 180 m deep, closed near its mouth by a sill about 50 m deep.
**Its deep water is replaced slowly.** Residence time is the volume divided by the exchange: a few months for the canal as a whole, about a year for the deep water at its south end.
**Decay uses up oxygen that nothing replaces.** Below the sunlit top, bacteria eating sunken plankton draw the oxygen down day after day, and the longer the water stays, the less is left.
**A fresh surface layer is a lid.** River water from the Olympics floats on top and keeps wind and tide from stirring oxygen down.
**New ocean water lifts the old.** In late summer the densest water of the year spills over the sill, sinks to the floor and shoulders the old, oxygen-poor water up toward the surface.
**A south wind finishes it.** It pushes the surface layer north, the lifted water wells up at the south end, and fish that crowded up toward the last oxygen have nowhere left to go.
**Human nitrogen is a small share in most of the canal.** It matters more at Lynch Cove, the shallow far end where water is replaced most slowly.
**The kills of 2003, 2006 and 2010 came in late summer or early autumn.** That is when the old water is at its worst and the new water arrives.

blocks.text: In September 2006, people along the southern reach of [[Hood Canal]], around the small town of Hoodsport on its western shore, began to find fish where fish do not belong. Rockfish, lingcod and other fish that keep to the rocks and mud near the bottom were hanging in the top few metres of water, barely moving. Divers reported dead fish lying on the bottom. Instruments lowered over the side measured the reason: below the top few metres, the water had almost no oxygen left in it.
It had happened before. A kill struck the same waters in 2003, and another came in 2010, both like this one in late summer or early autumn. Smaller episodes have been reported in other years.

Four things about it need explaining. Hood Canal is open to the sea, and the tide runs in and out of it twice a day, so it is strange that any of its water could be starved of oxygen. The trouble comes at the south end, far from the mouth. It comes at the end of summer. And it strikes within a day or two, after weeks in which nothing seemed wrong. Each of these has a cause in the physics of earlier lessons, and the last one is a surprise: the trigger is a fresh supply of ocean water.

Hood Canal is not a canal.[^name] It is a **fjord**: a long, steep-sided trough scoured by ice and then flooded by the sea. The Vashon ice sheet, which the Geology course follows south across the Puget Lowland, dug it. From its mouth near Foulweather Bluff it runs about 110 km (70 miles) south past Hoodsport to the Great Bend, then hooks east to Lynch Cove at Belfair. It is mostly 2 to 3 km wide, and its floor drops to about 180 m (600 feet) in the middle reaches.

blocks.caption: Hood Canal, from its mouth at the top to the Great Bend and Lynch Cove at the bottom. The dashed line marks the sill near the entrance.

blocks.text: Near the mouth the floor rises to a **sill**, a ridge about 50 m (160 feet) below the surface, like the ones that lesson 11 found at the Sound's narrows.[^sill] Behind it lies the deep basin. Lesson 12's two-layer exchange works here as it does in the Sound: fresher water leaves at the surface and denser ocean water comes in below. But only water from above the sill's crest can cross it, and once over, the inflow sinks only as far as its density takes it. Water denser than anything in the basin runs all the way to the floor. Water that is lighter than the deep water stops at mid-depth and slides in above it. So most of the year the bottom of the basin is left alone.

The rivers make it worse. The Skokomish, the Hamma Hamma, the Duckabush, the Dosewallips and the Quilcene run down from the Olympics into the canal and lay a layer of fresher, lighter water over the top. As lesson 6 found in Lake Washington, a light layer over a heavy one resists being stirred. Wind and tide churn the top few metres, where the water takes in oxygen from the air, but they cannot easily push that oxygen down through the layering to the water beneath. The fresh layer is a lid.

A useful number for any basin is its **residence time**: how long, on average, a parcel of water stays before it is replaced. It is the basin's volume divided by the rate at which water is exchanged, in the same way that a bathtub holding 200 litres, with a tap running 10 litres a minute and the drain open to match, turns over its water in about 20 minutes.

blocks.title: An estimate
points: Treat Hood Canal as a long box: 110 km long, 3 km wide and about 60 m deep on average. That is 110,000 × 3,000 × 60 ≈ 2 × 10¹⁰ cubic metres, about 20 cubic kilometres. Studies of the canal find its water as a whole is replaced in a few months. Four months is about 10 million seconds, so the exchange over the sill would have to average about 20 km³ ÷ 10⁷ s ≈ 2,000 cubic metres a second, the flow of a large river. The deep water at the south end sits off the main path of that exchange and is renewed only about once a year.

blocks.text: Water that sits for months would not matter if nothing used its oxygen. But something does. Each summer the sunlit top of the canal grows blooms of drifting algae, the plankton; when they die they sink, and bacteria decaying them use oxygen as they go.[^bio] Near the surface, the air and the algae themselves put oxygen back. Below the lid, nothing does. Every day the deep water loses a little, and the only fresh supply is new water from over the sill.

Oxygen dissolved in water is measured in milligrams per litre. Cold sea water in touch with the air holds about 9.[^mgl] Many fish become stressed as it falls to about half that, and below about 2, a level called **hypoxic**, most fish leave or die. The figure is a model of one deep basin: water arrives over the sill with the oxygen it brought, decay takes a steady amount each day, and the water is replaced at the rate the exchange allows.

blocks.caption: A model of a basin's deep water. The line follows a parcel's oxygen from the day it crosses the sill; the dot marks the residence time, when it is replaced on average.
blocks.task: Slow the exchange until the deep water becomes hypoxic

blocks.text: The rule the figure follows is simple: the oxygen left is what the water came in with, less the daily loss times the days it stays. Double the residence time and the loss doubles. A basin that is replaced in a month, like much of the Sound's Main Basin, barely notices its decay. A basin replaced once a year can use up everything it had. Hood Canal's south end is the second kind, and through each summer its deep water slides steadily toward empty. That explains the place and the season. It does not yet explain why fish at the surface die, or why it happens in a day.

Lesson 12 described the upwelling of late summer on the outer coast, when northerly winds pull cold, salty water up from the deep Pacific. By August and September that water reaches the Strait and the Sound as the densest water of the year, and some of it comes over Hood Canal's sill. It is denser than anything in the basin, so it does not stop at mid-depth. It runs down the slope behind the sill and south along the floor, a heavy river under the canal's old water.

blocks.caption: A section along Hood Canal from the sill (left, north) to the south end (right), through a year. Colour is oxygen. A model with depths and timing simplified.
blocks.task: Guess, then play the year with the inflow and a south wind both on

blocks.text: The new water does not mix with the old. It slides underneath it and lifts it, the way syrup poured into a glass of water goes to the bottom and raises the water above it. The water lifted is the worst in the basin: the oldest water, which has been losing oxygen since spring. As the new water piles up on the floor, that old water is pushed up until it lies just under the fresh lid, and the oxygen-rich layer the fish need is squeezed to a few metres. This is when divers see bottom fish crowding into the shallows. The new water itself is no great gift either: it spent a long time deep in the Pacific before it was upwelled, and much of its own oxygen was used up there.

Then the wind. A south wind, one blowing from the south, pushes the light surface layer north along the canal. Something has to take its place at the south end, and the only water available is what lies beneath. Lesson 6 found the same in a lake, where wind piling up warm water at one end makes the cold water below rise at the other.[^tilt] In an ordinary year the water that wells up is middling, and nothing much happens. In a year when the old water has been lifted to just under the lid, the water that wells up is the old water itself. It reaches the surface at the south end within hours, and the fish that had crowded upward have nowhere left to go. The kills have tended to come with exactly this pairing: low-oxygen water lifted high by a late-summer inflow, and a south wind to bring it up.

So the answer to the guess is that fresh ocean water, the thing that will eventually renew the canal, is what sets off the kill. Through the autumn the new water stays on the floor, the old water is mixed away by storms and carried out at the surface, and by winter the canal has its oxygen back. In a year with no strong inflow, the old water stays down, keeps losing oxygen and is not replaced, so the next year begins with a worse bottom.

Algae need nitrogen to grow, and more nitrogen means bigger blooms, more sinking dead algae and more oxygen used. People add nitrogen to Hood Canal: from the septic systems of the homes along its shore, from fertiliser on lawns and fields, from animals, all washed in by streams and groundwater. When the kills of the early 2000s made news, many people around the canal assumed that this was the whole cause.

blocks.title: A misconception
points: "Septic tanks made the dead zone." A study of the canal in the 2000s, the Hood Canal Dissolved Oxygen Program, found that in most of the canal the nitrogen from people is a small share of the total. Most of it comes in from the ocean with the deep inflow. The exception is Lynch Cove, the shallow far end past the Great Bend, where water is replaced most slowly and human nitrogen is a larger share.

blocks.text: The flushing figure shows why the place matters. Turn its decay up a little, as extra nitrogen would, and a basin that is flushed every month barely changes; a basin that keeps its water for most of a year loses a great deal more. Lynch Cove has low oxygen at depth almost every late summer, and there the nitrogen people add makes a measurable difference.[^lynch]

The canal is now watched closely. The University of Washington keeps moored buoys in it, at Hoodsport, Twanoh and elsewhere, whose instruments run up and down the water column several times a day measuring temperature, salt and oxygen. Their records show the year this lesson describes: oxygen falling in the deep water through summer, the low-oxygen layer rising in late summer as the dense water comes in, and the recovery in autumn. When the bad water is already high and a south wind is forecast, the people who watch the buoys know what may follow.

blocks.title: Outside
points: In late August or September, look up the Hoodsport or Twanoh buoy on NANOOS, the Northwest's ocean data site (nanoos.org), and find its oxygen plot by depth. Watch for the low-oxygen layer creeping toward the surface, and check the wind forecast for southern Hood Canal. If you visit the canal then, at Potlatch or Twanoh State Park, the water at the surface looks no different, which is the point.

blocks.caption: Six questions on Hood Canal
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why does the deep water at the south end of Hood Canal stay so long?
choices: A sill near the mouth admits only some of the ocean water, and the deep basin far from it is off the main path of the exchange
The tide does not reach the south end of the canal, so its water never moves in or out
The rivers at the south end push the deep water back toward the mouth so it cannot enter
The water at the south end is warmer than the ocean, so ocean water floats over it
items.why: Only water from above the sill's crest can cross, only the densest reaches the floor, and the far south end is renewed about once a year.

items.ask: A basin holds 20 cubic kilometres and exchanges 2,000 cubic metres a second. About how long is its residence time?
choices: About four months
About four days
About four years
About four weeks
items.why: 20 × 10⁹ m³ ÷ 2,000 m³/s = 10⁷ seconds, which is about 116 days.

items.ask: Which explanation is best for why oxygen falls in the canal's deep water through the summer?
choices: Bacteria decaying sunken plankton use oxygen, and below the fresh surface layer nothing puts it back
Warm summer water cannot hold oxygen, so it bubbles out of the deep water into the air
Fish in the deep water breathe faster in summer and use up all the oxygen there
Fresh river water carries no oxygen, and it sinks to the bottom in summer
items.why: Decay takes oxygen every day; the air and the algae replace it only near the surface, and the lid of lighter water keeps it from being stirred down.

items.ask: In late summer, dense new ocean water crosses Hood Canal's sill. What does it do to the fish near the surface at the south end?
choices: It endangers them, because it slides under the old low-oxygen water and lifts it up toward them
It helps them at once, because it carries fresh oxygen straight to the surface water
It has no effect on them, because it stays near the sill at the north end
It endangers them, because it is too salty for fish that live near the surface
items.why: The new water sinks to the floor and does not mix with the old; the oldest, worst water is pushed up to just under the surface layer.

items.ask: Why does a south wind set off a fish kill at the south end of the canal?
choices: It pushes the surface layer north, and the water beneath, already lifted, wells up to replace it
It blows warm air over the water, which drives the oxygen out of the surface layer
It piles the surface water up at the south end, pressing the fish down into the deep water
It stirs up mud from the shallow beaches, which uses up the oxygen in the surface water
items.why: Water pushed away at the surface is replaced from below, as with the tilted layers of a lake in lesson 6.

items.ask: What did the Hood Canal Dissolved Oxygen Program find about nitrogen from people?
choices: It is a small share in most of the canal, and a larger one at Lynch Cove, where water is replaced most slowly
It is the main cause of low oxygen everywhere in the canal, mostly from septic systems
It plays no part anywhere, because all the canal's nitrogen comes from the ocean
It matters most near the mouth, where the canal's busiest towns are
items.why: Most nitrogen comes in with ocean water, but in the slowly flushed far end what people add makes a measurable difference.

name.title: Hood's Canal
name.text: George Vancouver's expedition charted it in May 1792, and Vancouver named it Hood's Channel, after Admiral Samuel Hood; on his published chart it became Hood's Canal. The name stuck, though the water was never dug by anyone.

sill.title: Why fjords have sills
sill.text: A glacier scours hardest where its ice is thickest and fastest, in the middle of its trough, and less at the mouth, where it spreads out and thins. It often leaves a ridge of rock or of dumped sediment (a moraine) at the mouth. Many fjords, from Norway to British Columbia, have a sill near their entrance and a deeper basin behind it.

bio.title: Decay
bio.text: Bacteria break down dead plankton the way we digest food, using oxygen and giving off carbon dioxide. The biology is the next course's subject; here all that matters is that it uses oxygen at a fairly steady rate wherever dead matter sinks.

mgl.title: Milligrams per litre
mgl.text: A litre of water weighs a kilogram, so 9 milligrams per litre is 9 parts per million by weight. Cold water holds more oxygen than warm, and fresh water slightly more than salt: about 11 mg/L for fresh water near freezing, about 9 for sea water at 10 °C.

tilt.title: Why the deep layer tilts the other way
tilt.text: Wind drags the light top layer downwind, so the water surface rises slightly at that end. The extra weight of water there presses the boundary between the layers down, and at the upwind end it rises. The surface tilts by centimetres, the boundary by metres, because the two layers differ so little in density. Lesson 6 met the same tilt in Lake Washington, where it sets off a seiche when the wind drops.

lynch.title: Other basins
lynch.text: Hood Canal's pattern is common in fjords and enclosed seas: a sill, a lid of fresh water and slow renewal. Parts of the southern Sound's inlets have low oxygen in late summer for the same reasons, and the Baltic Sea's deep basins have gone without oxygen for years at a time between rare inflows of North Sea water over its sills.
